newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia cracks down on independent radio.
newsitem.headline: Croatia cracks down on independent radio.

text.p: Croatia's government moved to shut down an influential independent radio station in Zagreb on Wednesday by awarding its frequency to a rival which does not yet exist, an editor at the radio said.
The popular Radio 101 said the government-controlled Telecommunications Council gave its frequency to Radio Globus 101 which is being set up by a tycoon closely linked to the ruling HDZ party.
"It is a tragedy that after 12 years of fighting for democracy and civil society the radio is to be shut down like this," said Zrinka Vrabec-Mojzes, one of two editors-in-chief.
"But we are going to use all legal means to fight against this absurd decision."
She was among the founders of the radio which promoted freedom of speech when Croatia was part of communist Yugoslavia.
Radio 101 quoted a Telecommunications Council member as saying that it could not broadcast legally after November 30.
The radio was the first media outlet to let Franjo Tudjman, now president, to speak in public 1990 when he was branded by the communist state media as a "person with dangerous intents".
There was no official comment on the decision which follows growing criticism of autocratic rule by Tudjman's nationalist Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ).

A U.S. diplomatic source said Washington had stressed the importance of press freedom to Croatia and added: "We lent our support to Radio 101 and tried to help them, but it's too soon to say what the (U.S.) government reaction will be."
Vrabec-Mojzes said: "This is a victory of the radical right-wing faction of the HDZ, who obviously have not realised what this is going to do to the Croatian image abroad."

Listeners immediately began calling the radio with messages of support. A war invalid had a message to the authorities which summarised the public reaction: "You can take everything from us, but you can't take the Radio 101."
